# Summary

In this report, we analyzed data within residents and directors, and then compared the groups' (*i.e.* residents vs directors) to one another. 

We found significant differences primarily in how directors and residents perceive different aspects of burnout, which are outlined further in the analysis. Analysis within the residents and director groups individually found little to no significance. 

Significance was determined by adjusting for multiple hypothesis testing via the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure to control false discovery rate (FDR) for each family of tests: within-residents, within-directors, and cross-comparing the groups.

# Methods

We first tested for associations between questions and differences in means across groups (residents vs directors) using t-tests (for continuous variables) and Fisher exact tests (for categorical variables) depending on the type of question analyzed. Every question that was measured on an ordinal scale was converted to a Likert scale, and t-tests were thus conducted for difference in means. 

We computed Cronbach’$\alpha$ for burnout-related questions featured in question 13 on the residents survey (12 on directors survey) in order to gauge the internal consistency of subquestions. This was only done within residents.

When we found consistency within question categories, we conducted additional analysis to see if median composite scores differed by subgroups. We did this using the Kruskal-Wallis test, a nonparametric version of ANOVA.  

After conducting the composite score analysis, we looked to see if treating additional variables on a Likert scale were monotonically correlated with groupings.  Significance and directionality of the correlation was reported. 

<!-- For questions with multiple parts, we split them into individual questions (e.g. 13a, 13b, 13c...) to see if there were specific responses that were influenced by the grouping variable in question, which was the role (being a resident/director) in the case of cross-comparison, or information like program, experience, etc. -->

<!-- Finally we present data visualizations to summarize the results. Interesting plots and findings were placed in the "significant findings" section with all plots appearing in are in the Appendix. -->

```{r validation-function, echo=FALSE}
# when trying to cross reference one question (question1) by another grouping variable (question2) 
validation <- function(question1, question2, data){
  df <- data %>%
    transmute(
      response1 = .data[[question1]],
      response2 = .data[[question2]]
    ) %>%
    drop_na()
  
  
  # comparison_res <- df %>%
  #   group_by(response1, response2) %>%
  #   summarize(counts = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  #   group_by(response2) %>%
  #   mutate(percent = counts / sum(counts) * 100) %>%
  #   ungroup()

  table_comparison <- table(df$response2, df$response1)
  
   if (nrow(table_comparison) < 2 | ncol(table_comparison) < 2) {
    return(tibble(
      Question1 = question1,
      Question2 = question2,
      P_value = NA_real_,
      Significant = NA,
      test = "insufficient categories"
    ))
  }

  test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(table_comparison))
  
  if (mean(test$expected <= 5) < 0.8 | any(test$expected < 1)){
    fish_test <- fisher.test(table_comparison, simulate.p.value = TRUE)
    if (fish_test$p.value <= 0.05){
     significant <- TRUE
   }
   else {
      significant <- FALSE
   }
    return(c("question1", "question2", round(fish_test$p.value, digits = 4), significant,"fisher"))
  }
  else{
    if (test$p.value <= 0.05){
     significant <- TRUE
   }
   else {
      significant <- FALSE
   }
    }
  return(c("question1", "question2", round(test$p.value, digits = 4), significant, "chisq"))
}

```

# Likert Scale Analysis

Factor variables are now treated on a Likert scale and we conduct Kruskal-Wallis to determine if there are apparent conclusions to make on the directionality of the significance. 

## Initial Residents Likert Analysis

No tests within the residents group evaluated to be significant at an $\alpha$ level of 0.05. 

```{r likert-function, echo = FALSE}
likert_analysis <- function(factor_var, grouping_var, data){
  if (grouping_var == "gender"){data <- data %>% filter(gender != "Prefer not to answer")}
  df <- data %>%
    transmute(
      factor_var = as.numeric(.data[[factor_var]]),
      grouping_var = .data[[grouping_var]]
    ) %>%
    drop_na()
  kw <- kruskal.test(factor_var ~ grouping_var, data = df)
  return(c("factor_var", "grouping_var", round(kw$p.value, digits = 4)))
}
```

```{r res-likert-results, echo = FALSE}
res_likert_results <- data.frame(
  factor_var = character(),
  grouping_var = character(),
  P_value = numeric()
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(question_dic_res))) {
  res_likert_results[i, ] <- likert_analysis(
    factor_var = question_dic_res$question1s[i],
    grouping_var = question_dic_res$question2s[i],
    data = f_res_coalesced
  )
}

res_likert_results <- res_likert_results %>%
  mutate(
    Adj_P = round(p.adjust(P_value, method = "BH"), digits = 4),
    Sig_Adj = Adj_P <= 0.05,
    factor_var = question_dic_res$question1s, 
    grouping_var = question_dic_res$question2s
  ) %>% arrange(Adj_P)
res_likert_results %>% select(factor_var, grouping_var, Sig_Adj, Adj_P)
```

## Cross-comparison Likert Analysis

For the cross-comparison, we are not conducting the same test for each comparison. Since we're comparing the residents and directors' responses, both variables will be the same type (Likert or Categorical), so we will conduct the correct test accordingly: Fisher's Exact Test for categorical variables, and t-tests for Likert variables.

Many of the tests evaluated to be significant, indicated by a p-value less than $0.05$. The means of each group for each question is reported, as well as the confidence interval for the differences between the means.

```{r cross-comp-function, echo = FALSE}
cross_validation_analysis <- function(question1, question2, data){
   df <- data %>%
    transmute(
      question1 = .data[[question1]],
      question2 = .data[[question2]]
    ) %>%
    drop_na()
   
   if (is.character(df$question1)){
     table_comparison <- table(df$question2, df$question1)
     fish_test <- fisher.test(table_comparison, simulate.p.value = TRUE)
     return(c("question1", "question2", round(fish_test$p.value, digits = 4), "fisher", NA, NA, NA))
   }
   else if (is.factor(df$question1) | is.numeric(df$question1)){
     df <- df %>%
    mutate(question1 = as.numeric(question1))
    t_test <- t.test(x = df$question1[df$question2 == "Director"], y = df$question1[df$question2 == "Resident"], alternative = "two.sided")
     
    return(c("question1", "question2", round(t_test$p.value, digits = 4), "t_test", round(t_test$estimate[1],1),round(t_test$estimate[2],1), paste0(round(t_test$conf.int,2), collapse = ",")))
   }
}
```

```{r cross-analysis, echo = FALSE}

cross_results <- data.frame(
  question1 = character(),
  question2 = character(),
  P_value = numeric(), 
  test = character(), 
  mean_dir = numeric(),
  mean_res = numeric(), 
  CI_diff = character()
  
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(full_dic))) {
  cross_results[i, ] <- cross_validation_analysis(
    question1 = full_dic$common_qs[i],
    question2 = full_dic$role[i],
    data = full_named
  )
}

cross_results <- cross_results %>%
  mutate(
    Adj_P = round(p.adjust(P_value, method = "BH"), digits = 4),
    Sig_Adj = Adj_P <= 0.05,
    question1 = full_dic$common_qs, 
    question2 = full_dic$role
  ) %>% arrange(Adj_P)
cross_results %>% select(question1, question2, Adj_P, test, mean_dir, mean_res, CI_diff)
```

# Cronbach's $\alpha$ for burnout-related questions in residents

We computed Cronbach's $\alpha$ for burnout-related questions featured in question 13 on the residents survey (12 on directors survey) in order to gauge the internal consistency of subquestions. 

We split the nine subquestions into three groupings: 

 1. Exhaustion, comprised of feeling emotionally drained, fatigued, and strained
 2. Depersonalization, comprised of feeling depersonalization, callousness, and carelessness
 3. Personal accomplishment, comprised of feeling positive influence, confidence, and exhilaration.

When running Cronbach's $\alpha$, the exhaustion and depersonalization groups both had $\alpha$ > 0.8, while the personal accomplishment category was much lower at $\alpha$ = 0.509. 

The exact $\alpha$ values and groupings are reported below: 

```{r alpha, echo = FALSE}
#exhaustion related questions + new comparisons 
exhaustion <- f_res_coalesced %>% select(PGY_level, gender, program_type, working_hours_per_week, call_days_per_month, quality_life, consider_quitting, feel_strained, feel_fatigued, feel_drained)

#depersonalization related questions + new comparisons 
depersonalization <- f_res_coalesced %>% select(PGY_level, gender, program_type, working_hours_per_week, call_days_per_month, quality_life, consider_quitting, feel_depersonalization, feel_carelessness, feel_callousness)

#personal accomplishment related questions + new comparisons 
accomplishment <- f_res_coalesced %>% select(PGY_level, gender, program_type, working_hours_per_week, call_days_per_month, quality_life, consider_quitting, feel_confidence, feel_exhilaration, feel_pos_influence)

# levels for this question
levels_feel <- c("Never","A few times in a year","Once per month or less","A few times in a month","A few times in a week","Once per week","Every day")

# creating likert scale values 
exhaustion <- exhaustion %>% mutate(across(.cols = c(feel_strained, feel_fatigued, feel_drained), .fns = ~  case_when(
  .x == "Never" ~ 1, 
  .x == "A few times in a year" ~ 2, 
  .x == "Once per month or less" ~ 3, 
  .x == "A few times in a month" ~ 4, 
  .x == "A few times in a week" ~ 5, 
  .x == "Once per week" ~ 6, 
  .x == "Every day" ~ 7
)))

depersonalization <- depersonalization %>% mutate(across(.cols = c(feel_depersonalization, feel_carelessness, feel_callousness), .fns = ~  case_when(
  .x == "Never" ~ 1, 
  .x == "A few times in a year" ~ 2, 
  .x == "Once per month or less" ~ 3, 
  .x == "A few times in a month" ~ 4, 
  .x == "A few times in a week" ~ 5, 
  .x == "Once per week" ~ 6, 
  .x == "Every day" ~ 7
)))

accomplishment <- accomplishment %>% mutate(across(.cols = c(feel_confidence, feel_pos_influence, feel_exhilaration), .fns = ~  case_when(
  .x == "Never" ~ 1, 
  .x == "A few times in a year" ~ 2, 
  .x == "Once per month or less" ~ 3, 
  .x == "A few times in a month" ~ 4, 
  .x == "A few times in a week" ~ 5, 
  .x == "Once per week" ~ 6, 
  .x == "Every day" ~ 7
)))

df_cronbach <- data.frame(Groups = c("Exhaustion", "Depersonalization", "Personal Accomplishment"), Alpha = c(
  as.numeric(psych::alpha(exhaustion[,c("feel_strained", "feel_fatigued", "feel_drained")] %>% drop_na())$total[1]),

as.numeric(psych::alpha(depersonalization[,c("feel_depersonalization", "feel_carelessness", "feel_callousness")] %>% drop_na())$total[1]),

as.numeric(psych::alpha(accomplishment[,c("feel_confidence", "feel_pos_influence", "feel_exhilaration")] %>% drop_na())$total[1])
))

df_cronbach
```

## Item-total correlations for burnout-related subgroups 

Note that Spearman correlation is used here. Spearman correlation measures the strength of monotonic relationships rather than the strength of linear relationships.  

```{r, echo = FALSE}
print("Item-total correlations Exhaustion Group")
cor_exhaust <- cor(exhaustion %>% drop_na() %>% select(feel_strained, feel_fatigued, feel_drained), method = "spearman")
cor_exhaust

print("Item-total correlations Depersonalization Group")
cor_deperson <- cor(depersonalization %>% drop_na() %>% select(feel_depersonalization, feel_carelessness, feel_callousness), method = "spearman")
cor_deperson

print("Item-total correlations Personal Accomplishment Group")
cor_accomp <- cor(accomplishment %>% drop_na() %>% select(feel_confidence, feel_pos_influence, feel_exhilaration), method = "spearman")
cor_accomp 
```
<!-- I think we want to use spearman correlation here -->

Notable strength of correlation exists between feeling drained and strained (`r cor_exhaust["feel_strained","feel_drained"] %>% round(3)`), feeling callousness and depersonalization (`r cor_deperson["feel_callousness","feel_depersonalization"] %>% round(3)`), feeling depersonalization and carelessness (`r cor_deperson["feel_carelessness","feel_depersonalization"] %>% round(3)`), and feeling callousness and carelessness (`r cor_deperson["feel_callousness","feel_carelessness"] %>% round(3)`). None of the personal accomplishment correlations were notably strong. These numbers were calculated exclusively from the residents response to burnout-related questions. # Composite Score Analysis

For the exhaustion and depersonalization groups, since they saw a large Cronbach's $\alpha$ value, we constructed a composite score by placing the data on a Likert scale for each subquestion and summing the responses to each subquestion across each resident. We then compared the composite score to PGY level, gender, program type, weekly working hours, number of call days per month, overall quality of life, and frequency of considering quitting residency.

To visualize these relationships, side-by-side box plots were created to visualize potential differences in distributions for each grouping variable in question.  Notable box plots are included here, and all are reported in the appendix.  

To formally check for statitstical differences, We conducted a Kruskal-Wallis test (i.e. nonparametric ANOVA) to determine if there were statistically significant differences between groups. p-values and interpretations for significant comparisons are recorded below. 


```{r composite-score-analysis, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

exhaustion <- exhaustion %>% mutate(score = feel_drained + feel_strained + feel_fatigued)

depersonalization <- depersonalization %>% mutate(score = feel_depersonalization + feel_carelessness + feel_callousness)

#accomplishment <- accomplishment %>% mutate(score = feel_confidence + feel_pos_influence + feel_exhilaration)

exhaustion %>% drop_na() %>% ggplot(aes(x = call_days_per_month, y = score)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Exhaustion score vs Call days per month",  caption = "16-23 days is much higher than all previous groupings, with a median score 4 points higher than all previous responses") + ylab("Composite Score") + xlab("Call days per month")

depersonalization %>% drop_na() %>% ggplot(aes(x = call_days_per_month, y = score)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Depersonalization score vs Call days per month", caption = "16-23 days is much higher than all previous groupings, with a median score 7 points higher than all previous responses") + xlab("Call days per month") + ylab("Composite Score")

exhaustion %>% drop_na() %>% ggplot(aes(x = quality_life, y = score)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Exhaustion score vs Quality of life",  caption = "Score decreases as quality of life increases") + xlab("Quality of life") + ylab("Composite Score")

exhaustion %>% drop_na() %>% ggplot(aes(x = consider_quitting, y = score)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Exhaustion score vs Frequency of considering quitting", caption = "Frequency of considering quitting increases as score increases") + xlab("Frequency of considering quitting") + ylab("Composite Score")

depersonalization %>% drop_na() %>% ggplot(aes(x = consider_quitting, y = score)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Depersonalization score vs Frequency of considering quitting",  caption = "Frequency of considering quitting increases as score increases") + xlab("Frequency of considering quitting") + ylab("Composite Score")

kruskal_df_exhaustion <- data.frame(Group = c(rep("Exhaustion", 7)), 
                         Score = c(rep("score", 7)), 
                         Comparison = c("PGY_level", "Gender", "Program Type", "Working Hours per Week", "Call Days per Month", "Quality of Life", "Consider Quitting"), 
                         P_values = c(
kruskal.test(score ~ PGY_level, data = exhaustion)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ gender, data = exhaustion)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ program_type, data = exhaustion)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ working_hours_per_week, data = exhaustion)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ call_days_per_month, data = exhaustion)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ quality_life, data = exhaustion)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ consider_quitting, data = exhaustion)$p.value))


kruskal_df_depersonalization <- data.frame(Group = c(rep("Depersonalization", 7)), 
                         Score = c(rep("score", 7)), 
                         Comparison = c("PGY_level", "Gender", "Program Type", "Working Hours per Week", "Call Days per Month", "Quality of Life", "Consider Quitting"), 
                         P_values = c(
kruskal.test(score ~ PGY_level, data = depersonalization)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ gender, data = depersonalization)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ program_type, data = depersonalization)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ working_hours_per_week, data = depersonalization)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ call_days_per_month, data = depersonalization)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ quality_life, data = depersonalization)$p.value,
kruskal.test(score ~ consider_quitting, data = depersonalization)$p.value))

kruskal_df_exhaustion <- kruskal_df_exhaustion %>% mutate(Adj_P = round(p.adjust(P_values, method = "BH"), digits = 4)) %>% mutate(Significant = Adj_P <= 0.05) 

kruskal_df_depersonalization <- kruskal_df_depersonalization %>% mutate(Adj_P = round(p.adjust(P_values, method = "BH"), digits = 4)) %>% mutate(Significant = Adj_P <= 0.05) 

kruskal_df_exhaustion %>% select(Group, Score, Comparison, Adj_P, Significant) %>% arrange(Adj_P)

kruskal_df_depersonalization %>% select(Group, Score, Comparison, Adj_P, Significant) %>% arrange(Adj_P)
```

# Additional correlation analysis 

We are now treating variables "quality_life", "working_hours_per_week", "call_days_per_month", and "consider_quitting" as continuous on a Likert scale allowing us to interpret the directionality of the association. The adjusted p-value less than 0.05 indicates a significant relationship, and the Spearman's rho column indicates the direction and magnitude of the correlation. 

```{r Spearman-cor-test, echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(broom)
library(purrr)

variables <- c(
  "quality_life",
  "working_hours_per_week",
  "call_days_per_month",
  "consider_quitting"
)

results <- map_dfr(variables, function(v) {

  exhaustion_test <- cor.test(
    as.numeric(exhaustion[[v]]),
    exhaustion$score,
    method = "spearman"
  )

  depersonalization_test <- cor.test(
    as.numeric(depersonalization[[v]]),
    depersonalization$score,
    method = "spearman"
  )

  bind_rows(
    tidy(exhaustion_test) %>%
      mutate(Outcome = "Exhaustion", Variable = v),
    tidy(depersonalization_test) %>%
      mutate(Outcome = "Depersonalization", Variable = v)
  )
})

results %>%
  select(Outcome, Variable, estimate, p.value) %>%
  rename(
    `Outcome Measure` = Outcome,
    `Variable Compared` = Variable,
    `Spearman's rho` = estimate,
    `p-value` = p.value
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    `Spearman's rho` = round(`Spearman's rho`, 3),
    `p-value` = signif(`p-value`, 3)
  ) %>% arrange(`p-value`) %>% mutate(Adj_p = p.adjust(`p-value`, method = "BH"),
                                      significant = Adj_p < 0.05)

  ggplot(aes(x =consider_quitting, y = exhaustian_score)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.2) + geom_smooth() + theme_bw()
```
